grammar.title: Grammatik
grammar.rule: mein Koffer · meinen Koffer · meine Schwester · mein Foto · unser Vater · unseren Vater
grammar.note_en:
A possessive determiner goes before a noun and relates it to a person or group: mein Buch (“my book”), dein Buch (“your book,” speaking to one person), sein Koffer (“his suitcase”), ihr Buch (“her book”), unser Haus (“our house”), euer Haus (“your house,” speaking about a group that includes the listener). The relationship can be belonging, family or residence; unser Haus does not by itself mean legal ownership of the building. The photo is Emil’s, while the red book is Lina’s.

Choose the stem for the possessor, the person it belongs or relates to. Ich uses mein-, du dein-, er sein-, sie ihr-, wir unser-, and plural ihr euer-. Distinguish ihr as a subject (“you,” plural) from ihr before a noun (“her” or “their”). In Ihr Bruder ist Emil (“Her brother is Emil”), ihr refers to Ada. In ihre Stühle (“their chairs”), it refers to Ben and Mira together. Context identifies the possessor. The noun's own gender does not decide whether the stem is sein- or ihr-: seine Tasche (“his bag”) still refers to Emil even though Tasche is feminine.

Then choose the ending for the noun and its grammatical job. Nominative is the subject form; accusative is the direct-object form already encountered with den and einen. Masculine nominative has no ending: mein Koffer (“my suitcase”), euer Vater (“your father”). Masculine accusative adds -en: meinen Koffer (“my suitcase,” as object), euren Laden (“your shop,” as object). Compare Mein Koffer ist groß (“My suitcase is large”) with Du nimmst meinen Koffer (“You take my suitcase”). Do not use meinen as the subject form merely because the speaker is male.

Feminine nouns use -e in both nominative and accusative: meine Schwester (“my sister”), Ich zeige meine Schwester (“I show my sister”). Neuter uses no ending in those cases: mein Foto (“my photo”), Ich nehme mein Foto (“I take my photo”). Plural has -e in the forms shown: ihre Kinder (“her children”), ihre Stühle (“their chairs”). Euer drops its middle e when an ending is added in the forms used here: euer Haus, eure Mutter, euren Laden (“your house, your mother, your shop”). Unser keeps its written e: unser, unsere, unseren. The table collects the masculine forms actually demonstrated; this chapter introduces no dative possessives.

Bruder and Schwester mean brother and sister; Mutter and Vater mean mother and father. Kind can mean someone's child even when that child is already an adult: Emil and Ada are their mother's Kinder (“children”). The three people in the photograph are Emil, Ada and their mother. Their father is not shown. The photograph's year remains uncertain: Emil writes the guess 1990? with a question mark. The numeral is not a new German number-word exercise. Damals (“at that time, back then”) contrasts the old scene shown by the photograph with heute (“today”); the surrounding present verbs describe what the picture shows and what the characters see, rather than introducing a new past-tense paradigm. Jung means “young,” contrasting with alt (“old”) for a person. Lange means “for a long time,” describing sustained looking, reading or writing.

Lesen (“read”) appears as ich lese, du liest and sie liest (“I read, you read, she reads”); the du/third-person stem has ie. Schreiben (“write”) appears in du schreibst and er schreibt (“you write, he writes”). The story distinguishes saying a name, reading the visible name, and writing a new mark. Kennen means being familiar with a person, place or object: Ich kenne das Foto (“I know/recognise the photo”). It is not a rule for expressing every kind of factual knowledge. The chapter leaves the notebook's precise whereabouts open; knowing the photo and its people does not mean knowing where every associated object is.

In the reference table, Das Bild zeigt unsere Mutter means “The picture shows our mother,” and Wir sind ihre Kinder means “We are her children.” These examples use already encountered noun phrases and case forms.
